articles.title: Scientists just found a way to fight lung cancer and muscle wasting at the same time
articles.summary: A new nanoparticle therapy reduced lung tumors in mice while also targeting cachexia, the severe muscle wasting that can accompany cancer. By delivering follistatin mRNA directly to tumors, the approach could eventually offer a way to fight both the disease and one of its most dangerous complications.
articles.content:
Researchers at Oregon State University have developed an experimental treatment designed to tackle lung cancer and the severe muscle loss that can occur alongside it.

The research, published in the Journal of Controlled Release, uses lipid nanoparticles to carry therapeutic genetic material directly to lung tumors.

Nanoparticles Deliver mRNA to Lung Tumors

In experiments using mice, a team led by Oleh Taratula and Yoon Tae Goo of the OSU College of Pharmacy tested nanocarriers containing follistatin messenger RNA. The nanoparticles accumulated in lung tumors, where the mRNA instructed cells to produce follistatin, a protein that can help suppress tumor growth while also supporting the growth of muscle tissue.

The lipid nanoparticles, known as LNPs, are delivered intravenously. Their ability to reach lung tumors depends in part on vitronectin, a protein naturally found in blood serum.

Lipids are fatty acids and related organic compounds that include many natural oils and waxes. Nanoparticles are extremely small pieces of material, typically measuring between one and 100 billionths of a meter.

"We found that these LNPs bind vitronectin in the bloodstream, which then directs them to lung cancer tumors by interacting with integrin receptors that are overexpressed on the tumor surface," Taratula said.

Integrin receptors help connect cells with their surroundings and influence how cells respond to signals in their environment.

Overcoming a Major mRNA Delivery Challenge

Getting mRNA based therapies to reach lung tumors after being delivered through the bloodstream has been difficult. Conventional lipid nanoparticles often build up in the liver instead of reaching the intended cancer cells.

"Systemic delivery of mRNA therapeutics to lung cancer tumors has been a significant challenge in our field, and this work offers a promising solution," Taratula said. "Compared to conventional LNPs, which tend to accumulate in the liver upon systemic administration, our approach achieved an approximately 2.5-fold greater reduction in tumor burden."

Lung cancer is the third most common cancer in the United States and the leading cause of cancer death (skin cancer is the most common, followed by prostate cancer for men and breast cancer for women).

The American Cancer Society estimates that about 230,000 new cases of lung cancer will be diagnosed in the United States this year and that roughly 125,000 people will die from the disease. Overall, about 5% of people will develop lung cancer, with smokers facing a higher risk.

Targeting Cancer Cachexia at the Same Time

Lung cancer can also be accompanied by cachexia, a serious condition that causes severe weight and muscle loss. Cachexia can kill as many as 30% of the cancer patients it affects.

Unlike ordinary weight loss, cachexia can continue even when a person is eating enough food. Patients lose not only body fat but also significant amounts of muscle.

The researchers designed their treatment to address both problems at once by using follistatin mRNA, which has effects related to both tumor suppression and muscle growth.

"By loading our LNPs with follistatin mRNA, we developed a therapy that simultaneously targets lung cancer and cancer cachexia, all without adverse effects," Taratula said. "More preclinical work is necessary, but we're very encouraged by what we've seen so far and hope that testing in humans is down the road."

More Testing Needed Before Human Trials

The findings are still at the preclinical stage, meaning the treatment has not yet been tested in people. Additional studies will be needed to determine its safety and effectiveness before researchers can consider human trials.

The College of Pharmacy's Vladislav Grigoriev, Tetiana Korzun, Ammar Salem, Kongbrailatpam Shitaljit Sharma, Prem Singh, Chrissa Kioussi and Olena Taratula also contributed to the research, as did Daniel Marks of Endevica Bio, a company that develops peptide therapies.

Supporting the study were the National Cancer Institute, the Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development and the National Research Foundation of Korea.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific breakthrough in developing a nanoparticle mRNA therapy that simultaneously targets lung cancer tumors and cancer-associated muscle wasting (cachexia). This dual-action treatment has the potential to improve survival and quality of life for a large number of lung cancer patients, addressing both the disease and a deadly complication. The research is detailed, focused, and has broad implications for cancer treatment, fulfilling the criteria for inspiring good news with meaningful real-world impact.

articles.title: Cancer-fighting t cells burn out. Scientists may have found a fix
articles.summary: Cancer immunotherapy can lose its punch when tumor-fighting T cells become exhausted, but researchers may have found a way to keep them going longer. Scientists at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center identified a signaling molecule called MEK that can push T cells to burn through their energy while producing cancer-killing proteins. In animal and laboratory studies, blocking MEK helped the cells conserve energy, survive longer, and remain active even in the harsh environment around tumors.
articles.content:
Cancer immunotherapy can unleash T cells, the immune system's specialized cancer killers, against tumors. But there is a major limitation: These cells can become worn down before the cancer is eliminated. This condition, known as T cell exhaustion, leaves the cells unable to maintain a strong attack or keep tumor growth under control.

That problem has been particularly important for checkpoint inhibitors, immunotherapy drugs designed to remove biological restraints that normally limit T cell activity.

"A tragic part of T cell exhaustion is that the immunotherapy seems to be working for patients, and then it fades," says Santosha Vardhana, MD, PhD, a physician-scientist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSK) who treats people with lymphoma. "Many of them experience a brief wisp of promise only to have it taken away."

Researchers in Dr. Vardhana's laboratory have now identified a signaling molecule called MEK as an important driver of this exhaustion process. Based on animal studies published in Immunity, the findings suggest that blocking MEK might slow T cell exhaustion and potentially make immunotherapy more effective.

"We're excited about applying this finding to enhance multiple forms of immunotherapy," Dr. Vardhana says. "FDA-approved MEK inhibitors are already available, so this approach could be tested in humans without much delay."

How MEK Pushes T Cells Toward Exhaustion

Scientists have only recently begun to understand the processes that cause T cells to become exhausted. In 2020, Dr. Vardhana's laboratory identified an important piece of the puzzle: the cells' metabolism, meaning the chemical processes they use to turn nutrients into energy.

When T cells are continuously exposed to tumor antigens (the cancer proteins the immune system sees as foreign), the mitochondria inside the cells can become overburdened. Mitochondria are responsible for transforming nutrients into energy that cells can use.

"There is a large metabolic demand being imposed as T cells encounter cancer cells and try to produce cancer-killing, or cytotoxic, proteins," Dr. Vardhana says. "It turns out that the decision to make high levels of these proteins is regulated by MEK."

If MEK becomes excessively active, it can eventually drive T cells into terminal exhaustion, a severely depleted state in which immunotherapy can no longer reactivate them.

"We realized T cell exhaustion isn't simply a loss of function -- it reflects an imbalance between what these cells are being asked to do and the energy they have available," says Tanmana Mitra, PhD, a student in the Vardhana lab and the study's first author.

Surprisingly, the team discovered that exhausted T cells were not metabolically sluggish. They were actually highly active. When researchers treated the cells with MEK inhibitors, the T cells multiplied more while consuming less energy.

"That paradox made us ask where all that energy was going, and we discovered that these cells were investing enormous resources into making proteins," Dr. Mitra explains. "It changed how we think about T cell exhaustion -- from a problem of too little energy to one of excessive energy demand."

Helping T Cells Pace Themselves

The findings suggested that reducing MEK signaling could lower the pressure on T cells to continuously manufacture cytotoxic proteins. That, in turn, allowed some of the cells to stay active and capable of renewing themselves for longer, potentially extending the effectiveness of immunotherapy.

The concept is similar to pacing yourself during a long road trip instead of driving at full speed from beginning to end. Reducing the intensity can help preserve enough fuel to keep going.

In laboratory models, blocking MEK signaling allowed T cells to persist even in the difficult conditions surrounding a tumor.

But the researchers caution that suppressing MEK is unlikely to be the right approach for every cancer patient.

T Cell Exhaustion Can Also Be Protective

Scientists now understand that T cell exhaustion is more complicated than simply having immune cells lose their strength. MSK immunologist Andrea Schietinger, PhD, previously found that T cells can enter an exhausted state as a survival mechanism. By reducing their activity, they avoid becoming overstimulated and dying.

"As we've learned more about T cell exhaustion," Dr. Vardhana says, "we've increasingly understood that it's not the case that exhausted T cells are bad, so let's try to reverse the process with a drug. Instead, exhaustion is more of an equilibrium state that lets the cells survive and keep going -- almost like a 'safe mode' for T cells."

When a T cell is actively attacking cancer and producing cytoxic proteins, its mitochondria must turn nutrients from food into adenosine triphosphate (ATP). ATP is the molecule cells primarily use to store and transfer energy.

"Think of ATP as the currency in a fund that the cell spends down," Dr. Vardhana says. "If you spend ATP on one thing, you don't have enough to do something else. The exhaustion program is a sign that the cell's bank account is getting close to zero. MEK tells exhausted cells whether to conserve fuel or go for broke. What we found is that inhibiting MEK makes the cells more conservative -- helping them live longer while reducing the rate at which they produce the proteins that actually kill cancer cells."

That makes MEK both part of the problem and part of the solution. Strong MEK activity helps T cells attack at maximum intensity, but it can also push them toward complete burnout. Blocking MEK therefore involves a tradeoff: The immune attack may become less intense, but the cancer-fighting cells can survive longer.

Whether a short, powerful immune response or a slower, longer-lasting one is preferable may depend on the characteristics of an individual patient's cancer.

When T Cells May Need To Go Full Speed

According to Dr. Vardhana, MEK inhibitors would need to be used selectively. Two factors can indicate that a patient is likely to respond well to immunotherapy:

The tumors are small. The patients have a high number of immune cells attacking the tumor -- usually because the tumor has many mutations that make it recognizable.

"In these patients, conservation of T cells is not that important," he says. "It's like being in a car with 1/8 of a tank left, but you can see the finish line. In these patients, you would just let the car keep burning the gas -- in other words, take the traditional immunotherapy approach. These are the patients in whom MEK inhibition is probably not needed."

The situation may be different for patients with large tumors or relatively few tumor-fighting immune cells. Their immune response may not be powerful enough to eliminate the cancer quickly.

In those cases, creating a slower, sustained response with a MEK inhibitor could help T cells remain present for longer, even if they are partly exhausted. That persistence may be especially important when either the task at hand (the tumor) is large or the workforce (the number of T cells) is small.

Potential Uses Across Cancer Immunotherapy

Dr. Vardhana says carefully applied MEK inhibition could potentially improve several types of immunotherapy.

Checkpoint inhibitors: MEK inhibition has already shown effectiveness in melanoma when combined with checkpoint inhibitors and a targeted treatment known as a BRAF inhibitor.

Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy: "We think this approach could dramatically boost T cell persistence, which has been a big problem with CAR T cell therapy," Dr. Vardhana says.

Tumor infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) therapy: This treatment takes advantage of immune cells that have already been attacking a patient's cancer and expands their numbers. Using MEK inhibition before or after TIL therapy could potentially help the most effective tumor-fighting TILs survive longer.

Bispecific antibodies: These laboratory-made proteins are designed to attach to two different targets at the same time. They can strongly activate T cells, but that intense stimulation may also contribute to exhaustion.

"This study shows the importance of understanding core principles of T cell biology -- what sets the balance between conservation of energy and strong, cancer-fighting activity," Dr. Vardhana says. "Once we know the answer to that, the therapeutic possibilities really start to fan out."

Key Takeaways

T cells can become exhausted as they continuously recognize and attack cancer, reducing their ability to keep tumors under control.

The signaling molecule MEK appears to play an important role in pushing T cells toward exhaustion.

Blocking MEK may slow that process by reducing the cells' energy demands, potentially helping them persist for longer during cancer treatment.

The researchers suggest this strategy could be particularly useful for patients who respond poorly to traditional immunotherapy, including those with large tumors or relatively few immune cells capable of recognizing the cancer.

Additional authors on the study include Jahan Rahman, Madeline Hwee, Yan-Ting Chen, Ruben Jose Jesus Faustino Ramos, Hui Liu, Travis Hartman, Justin Cross, Miguel de Jesus, Morgan Huse, Valerie Longo, and Pat Zanzonico.

The discovery has broad implications for many cancer patients, especially those who respond poorly to current therapies, and is supported by detailed research and potential clinical applications.

articles.title: The top cancer success stories of the past 50 years, by the numbers
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 05 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03157-1Outcomes have improved drastically in the United States for some forms of the disease, but those for others continue to lag.
articles.content:
Improvements in cancer treatment in the past half-century have made many forms of the condition less deadly.Credit: Doaa Albaz/Middle East Images/AFP/Getty

An analysis showcases the past half-century’s biggest cancer success stories — but also highlights the recalcitrant malignancies that continue to vex researchers.

The report, released last month by the American Association for Cancer Research1 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, finds that 71% of people with cancer in the United States will live for at least five years after diagnosis, up from 49% in the late 1970s (see ‘Uneven progress’).

Among the success stories, gains in lung cancer survival rates are particularly striking, says Rebecca Siegel, a cancer epidemiologist at the American Cancer Society in Atlanta, Georgia. Lung cancer is one of the world’s biggest causes of death, and on average, only 13% of people diagnosed with lung cancer between 1975 and 1979 lived for another five years. Between 2016 and 2022, that number reached 29%. “It’s still really low, but it’s such an improvement,” says Siegel.

That jump in survival rates comes from improvements in surgical techniques and radiation treatments, as well as new medicines that either unleash the immune system against tumours or target cancer cells bearing specific mutations. “It’s very heartwarming,” says Michel Coleman, an epidemiologist at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine. Coleman says global statistics broadly exhibit this same trend towards greater survival.

Meanwhile, progress in treating childhood leukaemias is widely considered to be among the greatest achievements in cancer research. For children and adolescents up to 19 years old, the 5-year survival rate for lymphoid leukaemia has risen from 57% to 90%. That boost came not from the discovery of a transformative therapy, but from the careful, collaborative tweaking of dosages and timings for treatments that were already available, says Siegel.

Other highlights include liver cancer, for which five-year survival has tripled to 22% since the mid-1990s2, says Siegel. Survival rates for people with multiple myeloma, a type of blood cancer, have also increased drastically, in part owing to the development of drugs that harness the immune system.

Room for improvement
articles.reasoning: The article reports significant, measurable improvements in cancer survival rates over the past 50 years, highlighting major advances in treatment that have positively impacted millions of people. It focuses on concrete progress in multiple cancer types, including lung cancer, childhood leukaemias, liver cancer, and multiple myeloma, demonstrating broad and meaningful health benefits. The detailed statistics and expert commentary provide substantial context and substance.

La supervivencia al cáncer de hígado se triplicó al 22 %, y el mieloma múltiple también tuvo grandes avances debido a nuevos medicamentos inmunitarios. Estos avances significan que muchas más personas viven más tiempo y con mejor salud después del cáncer.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores continuarán desarrollando nuevos tratamientos y mejorando los existentes, enfocándose en los cánceres que aún muestran poco progreso. También trabajarán para que estos avances lleguen a más pacientes en todo el mundo.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Las tasas de supervivencia al cáncer en EE. UU. han mejorado mucho en 50 años, con avances importantes en varios cánceres gracias a mejores tratamientos y medicamentos.

articles.title: Medicine Nobel awarded for brain ‘switch’ that controls neurons with light
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 05 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03091-2Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel win the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for their work on optogenetics, which has revolutionized neuroscience.
articles.content:
Left to right: Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel were awarded the 2026 medicine Nobel on 5 October.Credit: L-R Stanford Medicine, Humbold-Universität zu Berlin/Philipp Plum, Robert Emmerich/Universität Würzburg

After being on many scientists’ shortlists for years, optogenetics — a technology that allows researchers to control the brain’s neurons with pulses of light — has been recognized by the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. The technique has transformed how neuroscientists study the brain, offering them a way to test cause and effect.

‘What took them so long?’ This year’s medicine Nobel winner is overdue

The winners are Karl Deisseroth at Stanford University in California, Peter Hegemann at the Humboldt University of Berlin and Georg Nagel at the University of Würzburg in Germany. They share the prize of 12 million Swedish kronor (US$1.2 million) equally.

Deisseroth said that, as a night owl, he had been working late before he received the call from the Nobel committee. “It was a complete surprise,” he told a press conference held by Stanford University today. “I was lying down, just starting to drift off to sleep, and my phone rang at my bedside,” he said. “There were about 30 seconds where I had trouble forming words … but [it’s] very exciting and overwhelming, and just delightful.”

A switch neuroscientists dreamt of

Neuroscientists’ aim is to unpick the brain’s many roles: how it governs feelings, behaviours and bodily functions. To understand how the brain works and how its cells mediate different behaviours, scientists require an approach that can perturb the system with high precision.

“Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of,” said Per Svenningsson, chair of the Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine, in the press release announcing the prize.

Working together in the early 2000s, Hegemann and Nagel discovered a light-sensitive protein called channelrhodopsin1,2 in the alga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, which is able to swim towards a light source. In response to blue light, the protein opens to allow charged molecules to flood into cells, creating a tiny electrical charge.

Can you name the women who have won a science Nobel prize?

In later work, Deisseroth and his colleagues inserted3 the gene encoding channelrhodopsin into neurons of rodents, and found that it caused the cells to fire and communicate with other neurons. The technology — a light-controlled ‘switch’ that allowed neuroscientists to alter specific cell types in the neural circuits of living brains using genetics — soon came to be known as optogenetics. It revolutionized neuroscience.

“We use light to turn on or off individual cells, or even types of cell or connections from one part of the brain to another. We can turn those on and off with millisecond precision in real time during behaviour, during cognition, and that allows us to see what actually matters for brain function and to start to map function and dysfunction precisely,” said Deisseroth. “It’s a real confluence of engineering and medicine.”

Illuminating the brain

The prizewinners’ work “fundamentally changed how we conduct neuroscience” and has “influenced fields far beyond it in biology, and opened new therapeutic possibilities,” says neuroscientist Rui Costa, who is president and chief executive of the Allen Institute in Seattle, Washington. “I first met Karl 23 years ago, and he was already thinking deeply about how to control the activity of specific neurons to understand and alter behaviour. Karl’s commitment not only to discovery, but also to sharing tools and reagents at scale, was equally transformative,” says Costa.

How to win a Nobel prize: what kind of scientist scoops medals?

The discovery and application of channelrhodopsin have led to a diverse ‘optogenetic toolkit’ that allows scientists in different fields to harness cellular activity with light.

Optogenetics has had a great impact on basic science, says Alexander Gottschalk, a neuroscientist at Goethe University Frankfurt in Germany. “It’s such an easy way, a very precise way, to define which cells should become responsive,” says Gottschalk. “Many people in the field have expected [this] for several rounds of Nobels already, but it took until now.”

Gottschalk has worked with all three winners, but knows Nagel the best. “He’s a humble person. He’s a modest person,” says Gottschalk. “I’m really happy that he received this prize today. It’s really well deserved.”

Into the clinic

Insights provided by optogenetic tools have helped researchers to better understand healthy brain function and conditions such as depression, schizophrenia, Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s.

articles.personality_title: Nobel Prize awarded for light-based control of brain cells
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists have long wanted a way to control brain cells precisely to understand how the brain works. Neurons, the brain’s cells, send signals that control feelings, movements, and thoughts. Until recently, it was very hard to turn these cells on or off in living brains with exact timing.

**What happened** – On October 5, 2026, Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for inventing optogenetics. This method uses light to control neurons. Hegemann and Nagel first found a light-sensitive protein in algae that opens channels in cells when exposed to blue light. Deisseroth then inserted the gene for this protein into neurons in mice, allowing scientists to switch specific brain cells on or off using light pulses.

**Impact** – Optogenetics has changed neuroscience by giving researchers a powerful tool to study the brain with great precision and speed. Scientists can now see how specific neurons affect behavior and brain functions in real time. This has helped researchers better understand brain disorders like depression, Parkinson’s disease, and Alzheimer’s. It also opens new possibilities for future treatments.

**What’s next step** – Researchers will continue improving optogenetics and exploring its use in medicine. The technology might help develop new therapies that target brain cells more precisely. Scientists also aim to map brain circuits in greater detail, which could lead to better ways to diagnose and treat brain diseases.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The 2026 Nobel Prize honors a breakthrough method that uses light to control brain cells, revolutionizing how we study and treat brain functions and disorders.
articles.personality_title_fr: Le prix Nobel récompense le contrôle des cellules cérébrales par la lumière
articles.personality_presentation_fr:

Jusqu’à récemment, il était très difficile d’activer ou de désactiver ces cellules dans un cerveau vivant avec une grande précision.

Hegemann et Nagel ont découvert une protéine sensible à la lumière chez une algue qui ouvre des canaux dans les cellules sous lumière bleue. Deisseroth a ensuite inséré le gène de cette protéine dans les neurones de souris, permettant aux scientifiques d’allumer ou d’éteindre des cellules cérébrales spécifiques avec des impulsions lumineuses.

Les scientifiques souhaitent aussi cartographier plus en détail les circuits du cerveau, pour mieux diagnostiquer et soigner les maladies cérébrales.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Le prix Nobel 2026 récompense une méthode innovante qui utilise la lumière pour contrôler les cellules cérébrales, révolutionnant l’étude et le traitement des fonctions et troubles du cerveau.
articles.personality_title_es: Premio Nobel por controlar células cerebrales con luz
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Durante mucho tiempo, los científicos han buscado una forma de controlar con precisión las células del cerebro para entender cómo funciona. Las neuronas, células del cerebro, envían señales que controlan emociones, movimientos y pensamientos. Hasta hace poco, era muy difícil activar o desactivar estas células en cerebros vivos con exactitud.

**Qué pasó** – El 5 de octubre de 2026, Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann y Georg Nagel recibieron el Premio Nobel de Fisiología o Medicina por inventar la optogenética. Este método usa luz para controlar las neuronas. Hegemann y Nagel descubrieron una proteína sensible a la luz en un alga que abre canales en las células cuando recibe luz azul. Deisseroth insertó el gen de esta proteína en neuronas de ratones, permitiendo a los científicos encender o apagar células cerebrales específicas con pulsos de luz.

**Impacto** – La optogenética ha cambiado la neurociencia al dar a los investigadores una herramienta poderosa para estudiar el cerebro con gran precisión y rapidez. Ahora pueden ver cómo neuronas específicas afectan el comportamiento y funciones cerebrales en tiempo real. Esto ha ayudado a entender mejor enfermedades como la depresión, el Parkinson y el Alzheimer, además de abrir nuevas posibilidades para tratamientos.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores seguirán mejorando la optogenética y explorando su uso en medicina. Esta tecnología podría ayudar a crear terapias que apunten con precisión a células cerebrales. También buscan mapear los circuitos cerebrales con más detalle para diagnosticar y tratar mejor las enfermedades del cerebro.

**Resumen en una frase** – El Premio Nobel 2026 reconoce un método innovador que usa luz para controlar células cerebrales, revolucionando el estudio y tratamiento de funciones y trastornos cerebrales.
